documents.title: Generative AI and ChatGPT Edu
documents.summary: A short Office of Academic Integrity notice issued with the ChatGPT Edu rollout. It says there is no university-wide rule: instructors set their own policies, students must confirm what is allowed, and AI work passed off as one's own is plagiarism. Instructors are encouraged to state expectations in syllabi and report suspected violations.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own for AI use: it says 'Instructors have the flexibility to set their own course-specific policies' and that students must 'confirm with their instructors what generative AI use, if any, is permitted', so the decision is handed to instructors and no tiers or templates are listed.

units.why: The page states that 'all active USC students, faculty, and staff will gain unlimited access to ChatGPT Edu'; this is a university-licensed tool offered institution-wide, so P92 (not P17, which is course-specific). It is a fact not a rule, hence informs.

documents.title: Generative AI General Policy
documents.summary: USC's formal Artificial Intelligence General Policy, issued January 2026 and revised September 2026, run by IT, cybersecurity and compliance offices. It sorts AI uses by data class and tool type into pre-authorized, prohibited and case-by-case, and sets duties on data protection, human review, procurement and agentic AI. It says little about coursework, pointing to student handbook and course rules.
documents.stance_why: The policy allows AI use under conditions: 'The following use cases for AI Tools are pre-authorized' and 'use of Enterprise AI Tools is encouraged', with prohibitions limited to controlled data and violations of other policy, so the stance is permit with conditions; it does not itself regulate coursework.

documents.title: Instructor Guidelines for Student Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: A February 2023 Academic Senate committee guide recommending that USC instructors set their own AI rules and tell students. It lays out two approaches, embrace and enhance or discourage and detect, with assessment techniques, sample disclosure language and a review of detection options and their weaknesses. It is early guidance that later integrity pages partly supersede.
documents.stance_why: The committee says it 'leaves instructors to set their own course policies regarding student use of generative AI' and offers two named approaches, 'Embrace and Enhance' and 'Discourage and Detect', so it sets no rule itself and delegates, with the two approaches listed as tiers.
